It probably means your gas system is tuned or specced for full power loads and the Tula just doesn't have enough oomph to cycle properly.

IMO, semi-auto guns need to be designed around the cartridge they are meant to use. The AR was designed around brass cased ammo (5.56x45), the AK-74 around steel case ammo (5.45x39). The .223 steel case ammo then is kind of a mutant as no gun was designed for it. As far as extractor wear, it is a noted problem with steel case ammo. The extractor lip is relatively small and OK on soft brass but banging into steel not so much. It is something you need to watch as extractor failure leaves you with a poorly proportioned club.

Wolf tends to be weaker and shoot slower, so if your rifle's gas system is tuned to not be overgassed with normal ammo, it might short stroke. If it is overgassed normally, you might actually enjoy shooting it more as the rifle could run softer with less muzzle climb.

The steel case also creates an issue with long strings of firing, then leaving a round in the chamber. The steel is coated in lacquer to prevent rust, and it tends to melt at high temperatures, so if you get the chamber hot and leave a round in it for a few minutes, the lacquer re-solidifies and the round will stick, making extraction more difficult. It also makes cleaning the bolt face and chamber at the end of the day a priority.
